meta.blurb: An imaginary glass lift waits on a dark rooftop. Noor says it can go as fast as she wishes, and Kit steps in. They pass the Moon, the planets and a black hole, then reach the edge of what we can see.
meta.bible: Noor: a calm, funny guide who loves the night sky and carries a flask of tea. Kit: a curious young traveller who asks the questions and keeps a notebook. Skylift: an imaginary glass lift that climbs from the rooftop of an old house in a quiet town and can go as fast as Noor wishes. Tour order: Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, the Asteroid belt, Pluto and the Kuiper belt, Comets, Voyager, nearby stars, Nebulae, Exoplanets, the death of stars, Neutron stars, Black holes, the Milky Way, Andromeda, deep space, the Big Bang, Dark matter and Dark energy, then home. Real facts used: the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away; light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second; the Sun is about 150 million kilometres away and its light takes about eight minutes to reach us; the Sun and the Solar System are about four and a half billion years old; Proxima Centauri is the nearest star after the Sun, about four light-years away; the Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across; Andromeda is about two and a half million light-years away; the universe is almost fourteen billion years old. Key terms: Gravity, Fusion, Hydrogen, Helium, Galaxy, Atom, Telescope, Asteroid, Crater, Supernova, Pulsar, Spacecraft, Planet, Orbit, Nebula, Carbon, Iron, Oxygen, Nitrogen, Magnetic, Atmosphere, Aurora, Eclipse, Tides, Apollo, Sunspots, Solar, Rover, Perseverance, Ingenuity, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Phobos, Deimos, Ceres, Vesta, Bennu, Hayabusa, Ryugu, Meteor, Meteorite, DART, Dimorphos, Chicxulub, Galileo, Galilean, Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Juno, Shoemaker-Levy, Cassini, Huygens, Titan, Enceladus, Triton, Uranus, Neptune, Voyager, Charon, Eris, Pluto, New Horizons, Kuiper, Oort, Halley, Rosetta, Philae, Heliopause, Alpha Centauri, Proxima, Sirius, Betelgeuse, Orion, Hubble, Webb, Kepler, TESS, TRAPPIST, Pegasi, Exoplanet, Protostar, Plasma, Corona, Spectrum, Photon, Quasar, Cepheid, Leavitt, Lemaitre, Rubin, Zwicky, Lensing, LIGO, Bell Burnell, Magnetar, Kilonova, Event Horizon, Cygnus, Sagittarius, Gaia, Magellanic, Virgo, Redshift, Cosmic, Microwave, Inflation, Quark, Neutron, Proton, Electron, Spiral, Elliptical, Nebular, Supergiant, Dwarf, Giant, Hertzsprung. Henrietta Leavitt, Edwin Hubble, Antennae, Triangulum, Milkomeda, Local Group. Voice: warm, wondering and clear; every number is real or marked "about"; no invented facts.

The Long Way to Another Star
Stars That Fell In on Themselves

beats.scene: Kit climbs onto a rooftop at night with a notebook under his arm
beats.summary: Kit climbs onto his roof at night and finds Noor, who offers him tea.

beats.scene: A glass lift stands on the roof, glowing softly beside the chimney
beats.summary: Noor shows Kit a glass lift, called the Skylift, that was not there yesterday.

beats.scene: Kit asks a question while Noor smiles in the lift doorway
beats.summary: Noor explains that the lift is imaginary but every fact on the trip is true.

beats.scene: Kit and Noor stand inside the glass lift with one large button
beats.summary: Noor says the lift can go as fast as she wishes, and Kit steps in.

beats.scene: The town shrinks below the lift, its streetlights glittering like spilled sparks
beats.summary: The lift rises and the town below shrinks into a patch of glittering lights.

beats.scene: The lift passes through white clouds with a faint grey mist on the glass
beats.summary: The lift passes through the clouds, which are made of tiny drops of water.

beats.scene: The lift rises above the clouds, with a snow-capped peak far below
beats.summary: Above the clouds the air is thin, and Mount Everest is far below.

beats.scene: Stars shine steadily in a black sky above a thin curve of blue light
beats.summary: At about 100 kilometres up the sky is black and the stars stop twinkling.

beats.scene: Kit presses his ear to the glass in the dark while Noor taps
beats.summary: Space is almost silent because sound cannot travel without air.

beats.scene: Earth's curved blue edge glows below the lift while Kit writes in his notebook
beats.summary: Below the lift Earth curves like a great blue ball, and Kit writes his first note.

beats.scene: A bright space station crosses the black sky above the curve of Earth
beats.summary: A space station passes by, going around Earth about every ninety minutes.

beats.scene: Earth floats like a slightly squashed blue ball with a tiny Kit in front
beats.summary: Earth is a ball about 12,700 kilometres across, slightly wider in the middle.

beats.scene: Blue oceans cover most of Earth while white clouds swirl over them
beats.summary: Water covers about seven parts in ten of Earth's surface.

beats.scene: Earth turns slowly with the line between day and night moving across it
beats.summary: Earth spins once in about twenty-four hours, so we have day and night.

beats.scene: Earth travels along a great curved path around the glowing Sun
beats.summary: Earth moves around the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second.

beats.scene: Earth leans over, with summer in the north and winter in the south
beats.summary: Earth leans a little, and this tilt gives us the seasons.

beats.scene: Invisible magnetic lines curve around Earth like a bubble in the dark
beats.summary: Earth's core makes a magnetic field that shields us from the Sun's particles.

beats.scene: Green and violet curtains of light ripple over the polar sky
beats.summary: Particles from the Sun hit the air near the poles and make an aurora.

beats.scene: A cut-away Earth shows a thin crust, thick mantle and a glowing core
beats.summary: Under a thin crust Earth has hot rock and a core as hot as the Sun's surface.

beats.scene: The dark side of Earth glitters with city lights and the Moon rises
beats.summary: On Earth's night side Kit sees city lights, and the Moon comes into view.

beats.scene: A grey Moon grows large ahead while tiny Earth hangs behind the lift
beats.summary: The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away, and light crosses that in a second.

beats.scene: The lift lands and Kit steps onto grey dust under a black sky
beats.summary: Kit steps onto the Moon, where the sky is black and there is no air.

beats.scene: A line of old boot prints stands in the grey dust beside a flag
beats.summary: Twelve people have walked on the Moon, and their footprints are still there.

beats.scene: Kit leaps high in the grey landscape with the black sky above him
beats.summary: The Moon's gravity is weaker, so Kit can jump very high.

beats.scene: Round pits of all sizes cover the grey ground
beats.summary: The Moon's craters were made by space rocks, and nothing wears them away.

beats.scene: Dark flat plains and bright highlands on the Moon seen from far above
beats.summary: The dark patches on the Moon are old plains of cooled lava.

beats.scene: The Moon in four shapes, from a thin crescent to a full circle
beats.summary: The Moon shines by sunlight, and its shape changes as it goes around Earth.

beats.scene: The Moon pulls a bulge of ocean water towards it as Earth turns
beats.summary: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans and makes the tides.

beats.scene: The Moon passes in front of the Sun, which shows a thin bright ring
beats.summary: The Moon and the Sun look the same size in our sky, so eclipses are possible.

beats.scene: A giant rock hits young Earth and debris drifts away
beats.summary: The Moon probably formed when a huge rock hit the young Earth.

beats.scene: A beam of light races across the black gap from the Moon towards Earth
beats.summary: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second, faster than anything else.

beats.scene: The Sun burns huge and gold ahead, with a tiny Earth far behind
beats.summary: The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away, and its light takes eight minutes.

beats.scene: A row of small Earths lined up in front of the enormous Sun
beats.summary: The Sun is a star, and more than a million Earths would fit inside it.

beats.scene: A glowing ball of gas with no solid ground and bright swirling surface
beats.summary: The Sun is mostly hydrogen and helium gas, and it has no solid ground.

beats.scene: Hydrogen atoms squeeze together in the hot centre of the Sun to make helium
beats.summary: In its centre the Sun joins hydrogen atoms into helium, making huge energy.

beats.scene: A single ray of light zigzags slowly through dense glowing gas
beats.summary: Light made in the Sun's core takes thousands of years to reach the surface.

beats.scene: Dark patches on the bright surface of the Sun with arching loops of gas
beats.summary: Sunspots are cooler patches on the Sun's surface, which is about 5,500 degrees.

beats.scene: A pale halo glows around the black Moon during an eclipse
beats.summary: The Sun's outer layer, the corona, is hotter than its surface, which puzzles scientists.

beats.scene: A small spacecraft flies through a shower of bright particles near the Sun
beats.summary: The Sun throws out a stream of particles, and one spacecraft has flown through its corona.

beats.scene: Green plants and a small child reach up towards sunlight on Earth
beats.summary: The Sun is about four and a half billion years old, and all life depends on its light.

beats.scene: Four rocky planets circle the glowing Sun at different distances
beats.summary: The four planets nearest the Sun are small and rocky, and all circle in the same direction.

beats.scene: A small grey cratered planet half in blinding sunlight and half in shadow
beats.summary: Mercury is the smallest planet, with a year of only 88 days.

beats.scene: Bright patches of ice in a shadowed crater at the pole of Mercury
beats.summary: Even on Mercury, ice has been found in craters that never see the Sun.

beats.scene: A bright planet wrapped in thick yellow-white clouds
beats.summary: Venus is the hottest planet, with a surface hot enough to melt lead.

beats.scene: A planet turns slowly backwards under swirling clouds
beats.summary: Venus spins backwards so slowly that its day is longer than its year.

beats.scene: A red desert under a pink sky, with a blue sunset on the horizon
beats.summary: Mars is red because its dust contains rusty iron, and its sky is thin.

beats.scene: A huge mountain and a deep canyon on the red planet's surface
beats.summary: Mars has the tallest known volcano, Olympus Mons, and a canyon thousands of kilometres long.

beats.scene: A dry riverbed with round stones and a small wheeled robot beside it
beats.summary: Dry riverbeds on Mars show that water once flowed there.

beats.scene: A tiny helicopter hovers above red dust beside a rover with a robotic arm
beats.summary: A small helicopter, Ingenuity, made the first flights on another planet.

beats.scene: Two small lumpy moons orbit above the red planet in the dark
beats.summary: Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos, shaped like potatoes.

beats.scene: A wide, loose ring of dark rocks floats between two planets
beats.summary: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter and holds rocks left from the Solar System's birth.

beats.scene: A large round grey world with bright white spots on its surface
beats.summary: Ceres is the biggest world in the belt, about 940 kilometres across.

beats.scene: A lumpy rock shaped like a spinning top with a small rock beside it
beats.summary: Many asteroids are loose piles of rubble, and some have tiny moons.

beats.scene: A small spacecraft with solar panels collects dust from a dark rock
beats.summary: Two spacecraft have brought back dust from asteroids to study on Earth.

beats.scene: A bright streak of light crosses a night sky above a quiet hillside
beats.summary: A shooting star is a small grain of space dust burning up in the air.

beats.scene: A dark stone lies on sand, its surface covered with a black crust
beats.summary: A rock from space that reaches the ground is called a meteorite.

beats.scene: A huge rock falls through a red sky towards the ground, long ago
beats.summary: About 66 million years ago an asteroid about ten kilometres wide hit Earth.

beats.scene: A grey, dusty sky hangs over a quiet forest with small furry animals
beats.summary: The dust darkened the sky, and most animals died, but small ones survived.

beats.scene: A telescope watches a small rock move across a field of stars
beats.summary: Telescopes now track thousands of asteroids near Earth, so we can look out for danger.

beats.scene: A small spacecraft flies towards a tiny asteroid in dark space
beats.summary: In 2022 a spacecraft hit a small asteroid and changed its path.

beats.scene: Jupiter fills the whole window with bands of cloud and a giant red storm
beats.summary: Jupiter is the biggest planet, more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

beats.scene: Swirling stripes of cream and brown cloud on a fast-spinning giant planet
beats.summary: Jupiter is a ball of gas that spins faster than any other planet.

beats.scene: A huge red oval storm swirls in the clouds beside a tiny Earth
beats.summary: The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has lasted for at least 150 years.

beats.scene: A small probe orbits above Jupiter's blue and white storms near the pole
beats.summary: The spacecraft Juno has orbited Jupiter since 2016 and found storms at its poles.

beats.scene: An old telescope beside a sketch of four dots near a planet
beats.summary: In 1610 Galileo used a telescope to find four moons going around Jupiter.

beats.scene: A yellow and orange moon with dark volcanoes and a plume of gas
beats.summary: Io, a moon of Jupiter, is the most volcanic place in the Solar System.

beats.scene: A smooth cracked icy moon with a hidden dark ocean shown beneath the ice
beats.summary: Europa has an ice shell, and under it a salty ocean that may hold more water than Earth's.

beats.scene: Two large moons, one icy and one dark with craters, beside the giant planet
beats.summary: Ganymede is the biggest moon in the Solar System, bigger than Mercury.

beats.scene: A line of bright fragments streams towards Jupiter and leaves dark scars
beats.summary: In 1994 a comet broke up and its pieces crashed into Jupiter.

beats.scene: Invisible magnetic loops surround Jupiter, with glowing rings of light at its poles
beats.summary: Jupiter has the strongest magnetic field of any planet, and glowing auroras at its poles.

beats.scene: Saturn floats with wide shining rings against the black sky
beats.summary: Saturn is the second biggest planet and so light that it would float on water.

beats.scene: Wide rings of ice grains and blocks seen edge-on and from above
beats.summary: Saturn's rings are made of ice, from tiny grains to huge blocks, and they are very thin.

beats.scene: A seventeenth-century astronomer draws a planet with strange ears
beats.summary: Galileo thought the rings were ears, and Huygens explained them in 1655.

beats.scene: A spacecraft with a large dish orbits Saturn among its rings and moons
beats.summary: The spacecraft Cassini studied Saturn from 2004 to 2017, then dived into it.

beats.scene: A small moon with thick orange air above a dark lake of liquid
beats.summary: Titan has thick orange air and lakes of liquid gas, and a probe landed there in 2005.

beats.scene: Fountains of ice spray from cracks at the bottom of a small bright moon
beats.summary: Enceladus is a small icy moon that shoots water into space from cracks near its south pole.

beats.scene: A pale blue-green planet tipped on its side with thin rings
beats.summary: Uranus was found in 1781 and spins on its side, so it has very long seasons.

beats.scene: A lone spacecraft passes two distant planets, one pale green and one deep blue
beats.summary: Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2, has ever visited Uranus and Neptune.

beats.scene: A deep blue planet with a dark storm and thin white clouds
beats.summary: Neptune is the farthest planet, with the fastest winds, and it was found by mathematics.

beats.scene: A small icy moon with dark streaks beside a blue planet
beats.summary: Triton orbits Neptune backwards and was probably a world from the Kuiper belt.

beats.scene: A small icy world with a pale heart-shaped plain, far from the Sun
beats.summary: Pluto was found in 1930 and is smaller than our Moon.

beats.scene: A scale showing eight planets and a small dwarf planet at the end
beats.summary: In 2006 astronomers decided that Pluto is a dwarf planet, not a full planet.

beats.scene: A spacecraft flies past a world of ice, mountains and blue haze
beats.summary: In 2015 the spacecraft New Horizons flew past Pluto and showed mountains and a heart.

beats.scene: Pluto and its large moon circle a point between them
beats.summary: Pluto's biggest moon, Charon, is half as wide as Pluto, so they form a double world.

beats.scene: A ring of small icy rocks around the Solar System's edge, far out
beats.summary: Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper belt, a huge ring of icy worlds, one of them shaped like a snowman.

beats.scene: A bright comet with a long glowing tail near the Sun, among dark stars
beats.summary: A comet is a ball of ice and dust, and its tail always points away from the Sun.

beats.scene: A bright comet over a medieval village and an old astronomer with a notebook
beats.summary: Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years, and Edmond Halley predicted it.

beats.scene: A small spacecraft hovers beside a rocky comet and drops a small lander
beats.summary: In 2014 a spacecraft called Rosetta put a small lander, Philae, on a comet.

beats.scene: A faint spherical shell of icy rocks surrounds a tiny Sun in darkness
beats.summary: The Oort cloud is a huge shell of icy rocks at the far edge of the Solar System.

beats.scene: A glowing bubble around the Sun with a small probe crossing its edge
beats.summary: The Sun blows a bubble of particles, and Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012.

beats.scene: A small old spacecraft with a dish glides through the dark between the stars
beats.summary: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object from Earth.

beats.scene: A shiny golden disc with pictures carved on its cover on the spacecraft
beats.summary: A golden record on Voyager carries sounds and pictures from Earth.

beats.scene: A tiny pale dot caught in a beam of sunlight in black space
beats.summary: In 1990 Voyager 1 looked back and took a picture of Earth as a tiny pale dot.

beats.scene: A glowing path of light stretching between two small stars in space
beats.summary: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, about nine and a half trillion kilometres.

beats.scene: A small faint red star beside two brighter stars close together
beats.summary: The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about four light-years away.

beats.scene: A grapefruit on a table and a tiny dot on a map far away
beats.summary: If the Sun were a grapefruit, the next star would be about 3,000 kilometres away.

beats.scene: A tiny spacecraft crawls towards a faint red star as pages of years pass
beats.summary: At Voyager's speed, the trip to the nearest star would take about 75,000 years.

beats.scene: A sky full of stars over a dark hill
beats.summary: Without a telescope you can see about 5,000 stars, and the brightest at night is Sirius.

beats.scene: A band of stars of blue, white and red shining in the dark
beats.summary: Stars have different colours, and the colour shows how hot each one is.

beats.scene: A huge red star beside the stars of a hunter shape in the sky
beats.summary: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant so big that it would swallow the planets out past Mars.

beats.scene: A glowing cloud of pink and blue gas with bright young stars inside it
beats.summary: Stars are born inside clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.

beats.scene: Dark lumps of gas fall inward and glow as they gather
beats.summary: In the cloud, gravity pulls lumps of gas together, and they heat up.

beats.scene: A bright new star shines in the centre of a ball of dust
beats.summary: A new star starts to shine when its centre reaches about ten million degrees.

beats.scene: Huge dark columns of gas and dust glow with bright stars at their tips
beats.summary: The Pillars of Creation are columns of gas where stars are forming, photographed by Hubble.

beats.scene: A tight group of blue-white stars shine together in a faint blue mist
beats.summary: Stars are born in groups, and the Sun probably began in a cluster too.

beats.scene: A spinning disc of dust round a bright star, with gaps
beats.summary: Around a young star there is a spinning disc where planets begin to form.

beats.scene: A rocky planet near a star and a giant planet far away
beats.summary: Rocky planets form near the star, and giant planets form farther out where ice survives.

beats.scene: A faint star with a tiny dark shadow of a planet crossing its face
beats.summary: In 1995 astronomers found the first planet around a Sun-like star, and thousands more since.

beats.scene: A space telescope watches a star dim as a planet passes
beats.summary: Telescopes find planets by watching for small dips in a star's light.

beats.scene: A small red star with seven small planets lined up beside it
beats.summary: Around the small star TRAPPIST-1, about 40 light-years away, seven Earth-sized planets circle.

beats.scene: A steady yellow star shines among its orbiting planets
beats.summary: Most stars, like the Sun, spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen into helium.

beats.scene: A small dim red star shines steadily beside a clock with no hands
beats.summary: Small red dwarf stars burn slowly and can live for trillions of years.

beats.scene: A brilliant blue-white star blazes with fierce light among dim neighbours
beats.summary: Huge blue stars shine very brightly but live only a few million years.

beats.scene: The Sun swells into a huge red ball and swallows the planets near it
beats.summary: In about five billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant.

beats.scene: A glowing ring of coloured gas surrounds a tiny white star
beats.summary: A dying Sun will throw off its outer layers and leave a small white dwarf.

beats.scene: A huge star has onion-like layers with a core of iron at the centre
beats.summary: Stars much heavier than the Sun make heavier elements, until their cores turn to iron.

beats.scene: A giant star explodes in a bright flash with colourful clouds of gas
beats.summary: The collapse causes a supernova, an explosion that can outshine a whole galaxy for a time.

beats.scene: Colourful clouds of newly made atoms drift away from a faded explosion
beats.summary: Stars make elements like carbon and oxygen, and supernovae scatter them into space.

beats.scene: Two tiny dense stars spiral together and burst in a flash of gold light
beats.summary: Heavy elements like gold are made when neutron stars collide.

beats.scene: Kit holds his hand up against a sky full of stars
beats.summary: Almost every atom in your body, except hydrogen, was made inside a star.

beats.scene: A tiny dense star the size of a city glows in the dark
beats.summary: A neutron star is the crushed core of a dead star, about 20 kilometres wide.

beats.scene: A spinning dark star sends two beams of light sweeping through space
beats.summary: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star whose beams sweep past us like a lighthouse.

beats.scene: A black circle swallows the light of a collapsing star
beats.summary: If a star is heavy enough, its core collapses completely and becomes a black hole.

beats.scene: A black sphere bends the light of the stars around it
beats.summary: A black hole has gravity so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.

beats.scene: A small dark sphere replaces the Sun while the planets keep circling
beats.summary: A black hole does not suck things in: if the Sun became one, Earth would still orbit.

beats.scene: A clock face slows and stretches as it nears a dark sphere
beats.summary: Near a black hole, time runs slower, and anything that falls in is stretched thin.

beats.scene: A bright swirling disc of gas glows around an invisible dark centre
beats.summary: We find black holes by the hot, glowing gas that falls towards them, such as Cygnus X-1.

beats.scene: Two black holes spiral together and send ripples through space
beats.summary: In 2015 detectors measured ripples in space made by two black holes crashing together.

beats.scene: A glowing orange ring surrounds a dark centre in a distant galaxy
beats.summary: In 2019 astronomers took the first picture of a black hole, in the galaxy M87.

beats.scene: Small and giant black holes lie in a bright galaxy centre among stars
beats.summary: There are black holes of many sizes, and giant ones sit in the centres of galaxies.

beats.scene: A wide spiral of billions of stars seen from far above
beats.summary: The Milky Way is our galaxy, with hundreds of billions of stars, about 100,000 light-years across.

beats.scene: A small yellow dot marks the Sun on a faint spiral arm
beats.summary: The Sun is about 26,000 light-years from the centre, in a quiet arm of the spiral.

beats.scene: The Sun circles the galaxy like a tiny bead on a huge wheel
beats.summary: The Sun goes around the galaxy once every 230 million years.

beats.scene: A pale river of stars crosses a dark sky above silhouetted mountains
beats.summary: From Earth the Milky Way looks like a pale band, because we see our galaxy from inside.

beats.scene: Kit counts on his fingers beside a vast field of tiny stars
beats.summary: Counting a hundred billion stars at one a second would take over 3,000 years.

beats.scene: A bright bar of stars crossed by two great curving arms
beats.summary: The Milky Way is a spiral with a bar of stars in the middle and a thin disc.

beats.scene: A round ball of thousands of old stars packed tightly together
beats.summary: Globular clusters are old, tight balls of hundreds of thousands of stars around the galaxy.

beats.scene: A dark centre with fast stars racing around it in tight loops
beats.summary: At the galaxy's centre is a black hole, Sagittarius A star, about four million times the Sun's mass.

beats.scene: A space telescope maps a field of stars in three dimensions
beats.summary: The Gaia spacecraft has mapped about two billion stars in the Milky Way.

beats.scene: Two small fuzzy clouds of stars shine above a lone tree
beats.summary: Two small galaxies, the Magellanic Clouds, circle the Milky Way and can be seen from the south.

beats.scene: The Milky Way shrinks behind the lift and a vast dark gap stretches ahead
beats.summary: Between galaxies lie huge, nearly empty gaps, and the nearest big galaxy is Andromeda.

beats.scene: A big spiral galaxy glows in the night sky above a mountain
beats.summary: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy with about a trillion stars, even bigger than ours.

beats.scene: A scientist looks through a telescope while a small star glows brighter and dimmer
beats.summary: In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed that Andromeda is far outside our own galaxy.

beats.scene: A star pulses bright and faint beside a notebook of old measurements
beats.summary: A woman named Henrietta Leavitt found a way to measure how far away certain stars are.

beats.scene: Two spiral galaxies drift towards each other across a dark gap
beats.summary: Andromeda is moving towards us, and the two galaxies may merge in billions of years.

beats.scene: Two clouds of stars pass through each other without colliding
beats.summary: In a galaxy merger, stars almost never hit each other because they are so far apart.

beats.scene: A spiral, an oval and an irregular galaxy float side by side
beats.summary: Galaxies come in three main shapes: spiral, elliptical and irregular.

beats.scene: Our galaxy and its nearest neighbours drawn as glowing dots in a small group
beats.summary: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group of about eighty galaxies.

beats.scene: Two colliding galaxies with long tails of stars and bright pink star nurseries
beats.summary: When galaxies collide, the gas squeezes and makes new stars, as in the Antennae Galaxies.

beats.scene: Thousands of galaxies form a web of glowing threads around dark empty spaces
beats.summary: Galaxies gather in clusters, and clusters form a web with huge empty voids.

beats.scene: A tiny dark patch of sky filled with thousands of galaxies of different shapes
beats.summary: In 1995 Hubble stared at an empty patch of sky for ten days and found thousands of galaxies.

beats.scene: A map of the sky with a tiny square holding thousands of galaxies
beats.summary: If a tiny patch holds thousands of galaxies, the whole universe holds hundreds of billions or more.

beats.scene: A blue galaxy nearby and a faint red one far away
beats.summary: Looking far away means looking into the past, because light takes time to arrive.

beats.scene: A huge golden mirror made of hexagons floats in space with a sunshield
beats.summary: The Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, sees galaxies from over thirteen billion years ago.

beats.scene: A rainbow of light stretched towards red beside a distant galaxy
beats.summary: As the universe expands, light from far galaxies is stretched to redder colours, called redshift.

beats.scene: Dots on a balloon move apart as the balloon is blown up
beats.summary: In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that galaxies are moving apart, which means the universe is expanding.

beats.scene: A galaxy and a ruler stay the same while space grows around them
beats.summary: Galaxies and planets do not grow, because gravity and other forces hold them together.

beats.scene: A ruler measures a galaxy while a speedometer shows two different numbers
beats.summary: Astronomers measure the speed of expansion in two ways, and the answers do not quite agree.

beats.scene: A priest in a dark coat writes equations beside a window with stars
beats.summary: In 1927 a Belgian priest and scientist, Georges Lemaitre, had already proposed the expanding universe.

beats.scene: Distant galaxies race away across a stretching grid of space
beats.summary: Very distant galaxies are carried away from us faster than light, because space itself is stretching.

beats.scene: A bright glow fills the whole sky, then fades into stars
beats.summary: The Big Bang was the hot, dense start of the universe almost fourteen billion years ago.

beats.scene: A bright point expands in all directions at once with no centre
beats.summary: The Big Bang was not an explosion in one place: space itself grew everywhere at once.

beats.scene: A dark question mark floats in front of a bright dot of light
beats.summary: We do not know what came before the Big Bang, or whether that question has an answer.

beats.scene: A hot white glow with tiny sparks that are the first particles
beats.summary: In the first tiny fraction of a second the universe was a hot soup of particles.

beats.scene: Clouds of tiny particles join together into the first atomic nuclei
beats.summary: In the first few minutes, hydrogen and helium nuclei formed.

beats.scene: A glowing orange fog fills space with no stars in it
beats.summary: For about 380,000 years the universe was a hot glowing fog through which light could not travel.

beats.scene: Light bursts free from a thinning fog and the first atoms form
beats.summary: After 380,000 years the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, and light could travel freely.

beats.scene: A faint glow in all directions seen by an antenna on a hillside
beats.summary: The light from that moment still reaches us from everywhere, now as faint microwaves.

beats.scene: Two engineers stand by a huge horn-shaped antenna on a grassy hill
beats.summary: Two radio astronomers found the cosmic microwave background by accident in 1965.

beats.scene: A colourful oval map of the sky with tiny warm and cool patches
beats.summary: Satellites have mapped tiny differences in the ancient light, the seeds of galaxies.

beats.scene: A cluster of galaxies swarms around a dark centre, with arrows showing fast motion
beats.summary: In 1933 Fritz Zwicky saw that galaxies in a cluster moved too fast for the matter we can see.

beats.scene: A galaxy with arrows showing fast stars at its edge
beats.summary: In the 1970s Vera Rubin found that stars at the edge of galaxies orbit much too fast.

beats.scene: A glowing galaxy sits inside a huge invisible ball drawn as a dotted circle
beats.summary: Dark matter is invisible matter that has gravity, and there is about five times as much as ordinary matter.

beats.scene: Pink gas in the middle, with blue dark matter on both sides
beats.summary: In the Bullet Cluster, collision tore the gas from the dark matter, which is strong evidence for dark matter.

beats.scene: A deep underground chamber holds a large tank, waiting in silence
beats.summary: Scientists look for dark matter with detectors deep underground, but have not yet found it.

beats.scene: A web of bright threads of galaxies on a dark scaffold of invisible matter
beats.summary: Dark matter acted like a scaffold, pulling ordinary matter together to make galaxies.

beats.scene: A single enormous blue star glows in a dark young universe
beats.summary: The first stars lit up about a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

beats.scene: Two teams of astronomers compare charts of exploding stars on a screen
beats.summary: In 1998 two teams found that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

beats.scene: A glowing arrow pushes galaxies apart across an enormous dark space
beats.summary: Dark energy is the name for whatever makes the expansion speed up, and nobody knows what it is.

beats.scene: A pie chart with a small slice of matter and big dark slices
beats.summary: Only about 5 percent of the universe is ordinary matter, about 27 percent is dark matter and about 68 percent is dark energy.

beats.scene: The glass lift hangs among faint galaxies, with no wall or edge in sight
beats.summary: Kit asks whether the universe has an edge, and Noor says there is an edge to what we can see.

beats.scene: A thin glowing sphere surrounds a tiny Milky Way at its centre
beats.summary: The observable universe reaches about 46 billion light-years in every direction from us.

beats.scene: Kit stares into dark space beyond the last faint glowing galaxy
beats.summary: Beyond the observable universe there is probably more universe that nobody can ever see.

beats.scene: A flat grid of light stretches away in all directions like a sheet
beats.summary: Measurements show that space is very nearly flat, which does not say whether it is finite or infinite.

beats.scene: Countless tiny stars scatter across the dark like grains of sand on a beach
beats.summary: There are probably more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches.

beats.scene: Kit holds out his hand in a vast, almost empty dark space
beats.summary: Most of the universe is almost empty space, with less than one atom in every cubic metre on average.

beats.scene: Distant galaxies fade slowly from a dark sky, leaving a few bright ones
beats.summary: In the far future, distant galaxies will drift out of sight, and the Milky Way will be mostly alone.

beats.scene: A last small red star glows faintly in a vast dark sky
beats.summary: Stars will keep forming for a very long time, but one day the gas will run out.

beats.scene: Kit looks at a small blue and white world among distant stars
beats.summary: Nobody has found life beyond Earth yet, but the ingredients and the places to look are common.

beats.scene: Kit writes in his notebook as a huge new telescope stands on a mountain
beats.summary: New telescopes such as the Extremely Large Telescope will keep pushing the edge of knowledge outwards.

beats.scene: The glass lift turns and heads back through the dark towards a small galaxy
beats.summary: Kit asks to go home, and the Skylift turns around.

beats.scene: The Milky Way glows as a spiral, and the lift drops to one arm
beats.summary: The Milky Way grows into a great spiral again, and the lift drops towards a quiet arm.

beats.scene: The Sun glows ahead as the lift passes the giant planets one by one
beats.summary: Kit says goodbye to Neptune, Saturn and Jupiter as the lift passes them again.

beats.scene: Earth shines as a small blue and white world against black space
beats.summary: Kit sees Earth again, small and blue, and knows that everyone he has ever known lives there.

beats.scene: Kit turns the pages of his notebook, which are full of drawings and numbers
beats.summary: Kit reads his notebook list: the footprints, old sunlight, rusty Mars and the ancient glow.

beats.scene: Noor and Kit sit on the lift floor, drinking tea
beats.summary: Noor says that people learned all this by asking questions, building instruments and being patient.

beats.scene: A boy with binoculars looks up at the Moon and the bright planets
beats.summary: Anyone can start: binoculars show the Moon's craters and Jupiter's four moons, and Andromeda is a faint smudge.

beats.scene: The glass lift settles gently onto the old roof beside the chimney
beats.summary: The Skylift lands on the rooftop, where the town is still asleep and the same stars shine.

beats.scene: Noor steps into the fading lift and leaves her flask of tea behind
beats.summary: Noor says goodbye, and the lift fades away, leaving the flask of tea still warm.

beats.scene: Kit sits alone on the roof, writing in his notebook under the stars
beats.summary: Kit is back on the roof, a small part of the universe that has learned to look back at it.

A1A2: Kit goes up on the roof with his notebook and finds a woman there.
Noor points to a glass lift on the roof that was not there before.
Kit asks if the lift is real, and Noor says the facts are.
The lift goes as fast as Noor wishes, so Kit steps in.
The lift rises without a sound, and the town gets smaller and smaller.
The lift goes through clouds, which are made of tiny drops of water.
Above the clouds the air is thin, and Mount Everest is far below.
At about 100 kilometres up, the sky is black and the stars shine with a steady light.
In space it is very quiet, because sound cannot travel without air.
Kit sees Earth curve below him and writes his first note.
A space station passes the lift and goes around Earth very fast.
Earth is a big ball, a little wider in the middle than at the top.
Most of Earth is covered by water, and the oceans look blue from space.
Earth turns around once a day, so some places have day and some have night.
Earth goes around the Sun, and it moves very fast, about 30 kilometres a second.
Earth leans a little to one side, and this gives us summer and winter.
Deep inside Earth, hot iron moves and makes a magnetic field around the planet.
Near the poles, particles from the Sun hit the air and make coloured light.
Inside Earth there is a thin crust, hot rock, and a very hot core of iron.
On the night side of Earth, city lights shine, and the Moon is getting closer.
The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from Earth, and light takes a second to get there.
Kit steps out onto the Moon, where the sky is black and there is no air.
Twelve people have walked on the Moon, and their footprints are still there.
The Moon has weak gravity, so Kit can jump very high.
Round holes called craters cover the Moon, and nothing wears them away.
The dark patches on the Moon are old, flat plains of cooled lava.
The Moon shines with light from the Sun, and its shape seems to change each month.
The Moon pulls on the oceans, and this makes the tides rise and fall.
The Moon and Sun look the same size, so the Moon can hide the Sun.
Most scientists think the Moon formed when a huge rock hit the young Earth.
Light moves very fast, about 300,000 kilometres in one second.
The Sun is far from Earth, and its light takes about eight minutes to arrive.
The Sun is a star, and more than a million Earths could fit inside it.
The Sun is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and it has no solid ground.
In the middle of the Sun, hydrogen atoms join together and make helium and light.
Light from the Sun's centre takes many thousands of years to reach the surface.
The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, and sunspots are cooler dark patches.
The Sun's outer layer, the corona, is much hotter than its surface.
The Sun throws out particles, and in 2021 a spacecraft flew into its corona.
The Sun is very old, and all life on Earth needs its light.
The four planets nearest the Sun are small and made of rock.
Mercury is the smallest planet, and it is very close to the Sun.
On Mercury, there is ice in deep craters that the Sun never reaches.
Venus is wrapped in thick clouds, and it is the hottest planet of all.
Venus spins backwards, and one day there is longer than one year.
Mars looks red because its dust is rusty, and its air is very thin.
Mars has a huge mountain called Olympus Mons and a very long canyon.
Mars has dry river beds, so water once flowed on the planet.
A small helicopter called Ingenuity flew on Mars, the first flight on another planet.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, that look like potatoes.
The asteroid belt is a wide ring of rocks between Mars and Jupiter.
Ceres is the biggest world in the asteroid belt, and it has bright spots.
Many asteroids are loose piles of rubble, and some have small moons.
Two spacecraft brought back dust from asteroids for scientists on Earth.
A shooting star is a tiny grain of space dust that burns in the air.
A rock from space that falls to the ground is called a meteorite.
About 66 million years ago, an asteroid hit Earth, and the dinosaurs died out.
The dust hid the Sun, and many animals died, but small ones lived.
Telescopes now watch thousands of asteroids that pass near Earth.
In 2022 a spacecraft hit a small asteroid and changed how it moved.
Jupiter is the biggest planet, and more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.
Jupiter is a ball of gas, and it spins faster than any other planet.
The Great Red Spot is a giant storm, bigger than Earth, and it is very old.
The spacecraft Juno has circled Jupiter since 2016 to study its clouds and its inside.
In 1610 Galileo used a telescope and found four moons circling Jupiter.
Io is a moon of Jupiter, and it has hundreds of active volcanoes.
Europa is covered in ice, and below the ice there is a deep ocean.
Ganymede is the biggest moon in the Solar System, and it is bigger than Mercury.
In 1994 a broken comet crashed into Jupiter, and people watched it.
Jupiter has a very strong magnetic field, and it makes auroras at the poles.
Saturn is a huge planet, but it is so light that it would float on water.
Saturn's rings are made of ice, in pieces from tiny grains to big blocks.
Galileo saw the rings in 1610 but did not understand them, and Huygens did in 1655.
The spacecraft Cassini studied Saturn for thirteen years and then dived into it.
Titan has thick orange air and lakes of liquid gas, and a probe landed there.
Enceladus is a small icy moon, and it shoots jets of water into space.
Uranus was found in 1781, and it spins on its side.
Only one spacecraft has visited Uranus and Neptune, and it was Voyager 2.
Neptune is the last planet, it has very fast winds, and it was found by mathematics.
Triton goes around Neptune backwards, and it was probably captured by Neptune.
Pluto is a small, cold world, and it is smaller than our Moon.
In 2006 astronomers said that Pluto is a dwarf planet, not a full planet.
In 2015 a spacecraft called New Horizons flew past Pluto and sent home pictures.
Pluto's biggest moon, Charon, is half as wide as Pluto itself.
Beyond Neptune is the Kuiper belt, a huge ring of icy rocks.
A comet is ice and dust, and its tail points away from the Sun.
Halley's Comet comes back about every 76 years, and a man predicted it.
In 2014 the spacecraft Rosetta dropped a small lander onto a comet.
The Oort cloud may be a huge shell of icy rocks around the Solar System.
The Sun blows a huge bubble of particles into space, and its edge is far away.
Voyager 1 was launched in 1977, and it is now farther from Earth than anything else we made.
Voyager carries a golden record with sounds and pictures from Earth.
In 1990 Voyager 1 looked back and took a picture that shows Earth as a tiny dot.
A light-year is how far light goes in one year.
The nearest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about four light-years away.
If the Sun were a small fruit, the next star would be far away.
At Voyager's speed, a trip to the nearest star would take about 75,000 years.
You can see about 5,000 stars without a telescope, and Sirius is the brightest.
Stars have different colours, and the colour shows how hot each one is.
Betelgeuse is a huge red star in the constellation Orion.
Stars are born in huge clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.
In the cloud, gravity pulls gas into lumps, and the lumps get hot.
When its centre is hot enough, a star starts fusion and begins to shine.
The Pillars of Creation are columns of gas and dust where new stars are forming.
Stars are born in groups, and the Sun probably began in a group too.
Around a young star, a spinning disc of dust and gas forms planets.
Near a star, only rock can survive the heat, but farther away ice can too.
In 1995 astronomers found a planet around another star like the Sun.
A planet passing in front of a star makes the star dim a little.
Seven Earth-sized planets circle a small red star called TRAPPIST-1.
Most stars, like the Sun, spend most of their lives making energy from hydrogen.
Small red dwarf stars burn their fuel slowly and can live for trillions of years.
Giant blue stars shine fiercely, but they live only a few million years.
In about five billion years the Sun will become a huge red star.
A dying Sun will throw off its outer layers and leave a small, hot white dwarf.
Very big stars make heavier atoms in layers, and the last one is iron.
The collapse causes an explosion called a supernova, which is very bright.
Stars make carbon and oxygen, and when they explode they scatter them.
Gold and other heavy elements are made when two dead stars crash together.
Almost every atom in your body, except hydrogen, was made inside a star.
A neutron star is the tiny, heavy core of a dead star.
A pulsar is a neutron star that spins, and its beams flash like a lighthouse.
A very big star can fall in on itself and make a black hole.
A black hole pulls so strongly that not even light can get out.
A black hole does not suck things in like a vacuum cleaner.
Near a black hole, time runs more slowly, and things that fall in are stretched.
We cannot see a black hole, but we can see hot gas falling towards it.
In 2015 scientists measured ripples in space from two black holes crashing.
In 2019 scientists showed the first picture of a black hole.
There are small black holes and giant black holes, and giant ones sit in galaxies.
The Milky Way is our galaxy, and it is about 100,000 light-years across.
The Sun is far from the centre, in a quiet arm of the galaxy.
The Sun goes around the centre of the galaxy once every 230 million years.
From Earth, the Milky Way looks like a pale band of light in the sky.
Counting a hundred billion stars, one every second, would take over 3,000 years.
The Milky Way is a flat spiral with a bar of stars in the middle.
Globular clusters are tight balls of very old stars that circle the galaxy.
At the centre of the Milky Way sits a giant black hole.
The Gaia spacecraft has made a map of about two billion stars.
Two small galaxies, the Magellanic Clouds, circle the Milky Way.
The lift crosses a huge empty gap to reach the Andromeda galaxy.
Andromeda is a spiral galaxy with about a trillion stars.
In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed that Andromeda is far outside the Milky Way.
Leavitt found a way to measure how far away some stars are.
Andromeda is coming closer, and the two galaxies may merge in billions of years.
In a galaxy merger, stars almost never collide because the gaps are huge.
Galaxies have three main shapes: spiral, oval and irregular.
The Milky Way belongs to a small group of about eighty galaxies.
When galaxies crash together, new stars are born, as in the Antennae Galaxies.
Galaxies gather in clusters, and clusters join in a huge web.
In 1995 the Hubble telescope looked at an empty patch of sky for ten days.
If one tiny patch has so many galaxies, the whole sky has far more.
Looking far away means looking into the past, because light takes time to arrive.
The Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, can see the first galaxies.
As the universe grows, the light from far galaxies turns red.
In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that most galaxies are moving away from us.
Galaxies and planets do not grow, because gravity holds them together.
Two ways of measuring the speed of expansion give answers that do not quite agree.
Two years before Hubble, a Belgian scientist and priest suggested the universe is expanding.
Very far galaxies move away faster than light, because space is stretching.
The Big Bang was the hot start of the universe, almost fourteen billion years ago.
The Big Bang did not happen in one place, but everywhere at once.
We do not know what came before the Big Bang, or if that question makes sense.
In the first second, the universe was very hot, and it was full of tiny particles.
In the first minutes, the universe made hydrogen and helium.
For about 380,000 years the universe was like a hot, glowing fog.
After 380,000 years it was cool enough for atoms to form, and light flew free.
The light from that moment still reaches us, as faint microwaves.
In 1965 two radio astronomers found this glow by accident.
Satellites have mapped tiny differences in that light, and they became galaxies.
In 1933 Fritz Zwicky saw that galaxies in a cluster moved too fast.
In the 1970s Vera Rubin found that stars at the edge of galaxies move too fast.
Dark matter cannot be seen, but its gravity is felt, and there is a lot.
In the Bullet Cluster, two galaxy groups crashed, and the dark matter and the gas separated.
Scientists look for dark matter with detectors deep underground, but they have not found it.
Dark matter pulled ordinary matter together, and it helped galaxies to form.
The first stars lit up a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.
In 1998 two teams found that the universe is expanding faster and faster.
Dark energy makes the universe grow faster, but nobody knows what it is.
Only five parts in a hundred of the universe is ordinary matter.
Kit asks if the universe has an edge, and Noor says no.
We can see far, but not forever, in every direction.
There is probably more universe beyond, but we cannot see it.
Space looks flat, but we do not know if it is endless.
There are probably more stars than grains of sand on Earth.
Most of space is almost empty, with very few atoms.
Far in the future, other galaxies will move away and fade from view.
Stars will keep forming for a long time, but not forever.
Nobody has found life on another world yet, but we are looking.
Kit writes that new telescopes will keep moving the edge outwards.
Kit says he is ready, and the lift turns around.
The Milky Way grows large again, and the lift goes towards one arm.
Kit waves to Neptune, Saturn and Jupiter as the lift passes.
Earth looks small and blue, and everyone Kit knows lives there.
Kit reads the list in his notebook out loud to Noor.
Noor says people learned all this by asking questions and being patient.
You can see the Moon's craters and Jupiter's moons with small telescopes.
The lift lands on the roof, and the town is still asleep.
Noor says goodbye, and the lift fades away, but the tea is still warm.
Kit is alone on the roof, a small part of the universe that can ask questions.
B1B2: Kit had climbed onto the old roof with his notebook to watch the stars, and he was surprised to find someone already there. A woman sat by the chimney with a flask of tea and a calm smile.
Noor pointed behind him, and Kit saw a tall glass lift glowing softly on the roof. It had certainly not been there the day before, and its door was already open.

Kit asked whether the lift was real, and Noor admitted that it was only imagined. However, she promised that every fact they met on the journey would be true, because the universe needs no help from made-up stories.

The Skylift, Noor explained, could travel as fast as she wished, so even the longest distances could be crossed in a few minutes. Kit took a deep breath, stepped inside and watched the door slide quietly shut behind him.
Without any noise at all, the Skylift began to rise. Kit watched his street, his school and the park shrink until the whole town was only a small patch of glittering lights.
Soon the lift slid into a cloud, and a cool grey mist pressed against the glass. Noor said clouds are billions of tiny water drops, and most stay within twelve kilometres of the ground.

Above the clouds the air became thin and the stars grew brighter. Far below them stood the top of Mount Everest, which is about nine kilometres high, and Noor said that even there climbers struggle to breathe.

At about 100 kilometres above the ground, the sky turned completely black. Noor explained that stars twinkle only because their light wobbles as it passes through air, so up here they shone steadily instead.
Kit tapped the glass and heard nothing at all. Noor said sound is a shaking of air, and in the near-empty space outside it has nothing to shake.
Below them the edge of the Earth curved away, bright with blue light, and Kit felt his stomach flutter. He opened his notebook and wrote one line at the top of the page: ask everything.

A bright shape flashed past the lift: it was the International Space Station, about 400 kilometres above the ground. It circles the whole Earth about every ninety minutes, so its crew see many sunrises each day.
From here Earth looked like a perfect ball, but Noor said it is a little wider in the middle than from pole to pole. It is about 12,700 kilometres across, and the lift seemed tiny against it.

Most of what Kit saw was blue, because oceans cover about seven parts in every ten of Earth's surface. The land looked small by comparison, and Noor joked that the planet should really be called Ocean.
Noor told him that Earth spins once about every twenty-four hours, which is why there is day and night. At the equator the ground moves at more than 1,600 kilometres an hour, yet nobody feels it.
As well as spinning, Earth travels around the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. One complete trip takes about 365 days, and that is what we call a year.
Earth leans over by about twenty-three degrees as it goes around the Sun. This tilt gives us the seasons, so when it is summer in the north, it is winter in the south.

Deep inside Earth, a core of hot, liquid iron moves and swirls, and this movement makes a magnetic field around the whole planet. The field acts like a shield, turning away many of the fast particles that stream out from the Sun.
Some particles from the Sun slip in near the poles and crash into the air, which makes it glow. This is an aurora, and the green colour comes from oxygen high above the ground.

Noor drew a picture in the air of what lies under our feet: a thin crust, hot rock and an iron core. The very centre is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, and it lies about 6,400 kilometres below us.

Over the dark side of Earth, Kit saw thousands of city lights glittering like a second set of stars. Earth is the only place we know of that has life, Noor said, and that life covers the surface like a thin green film.

Their first stop was the Moon, which hangs about 384,000 kilometres from Earth, far enough to hold about thirty Earths side by side. Light crosses that gap in a little over a second, but a car would need more than five months.
Kit stepped onto the Moon and his boots sank into soft grey dust. The Moon is a little more than a quarter as wide as Earth, and it has no air, no wind and no weather at all.
Noor showed him a line of old boot prints in the dust. They were left by astronauts of the Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972, and twelve people in all have walked here.
Gravity is the pull that holds us to a planet, and the Moon's pull is only about one sixth of Earth's. Kit gave a little jump and floated up far higher than he could ever jump at home.
The round holes all around them are craters, made when space rocks crashed into the Moon. Because there is no wind or rain, the craters are not worn away, and some of them are billions of years old.

From Earth, the dark patches on the Moon look like a face, but they are really wide plains of lava that cooled long ago. The Moon also keeps the same side towards us, because it turns once in the time it takes to go around Earth.

The Moon makes no light of its own, and it only shines because sunlight bounces off its surface. As it travels around Earth, we see more or less of its lit half, so it seems to change shape each month.
The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and raises a bulge of water on the side facing it. As Earth turns, most coasts have two high tides and two low tides every day.

By strange luck, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also about 400 times further away. This makes them look almost the same size, so sometimes the Moon covers the Sun completely and day turns to night.
About four and a half billion years ago, most scientists think, a planet-sized rock hit the young Earth. The broken pieces joined together and became the Moon.
Noor told Kit that light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second. In one second a beam of light could go around the whole Earth about seven times, and nothing in the universe is faster.

The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from Earth, and even light needs about eight minutes to make that journey. Noor said that if the Sun vanished, we would not know about it for eight whole minutes.
The Sun is a star, a huge ball of hot gas that is about 109 times wider than Earth. More than a million Earths could fit inside it, and it holds nearly all the mass of the Solar System.
The Sun is made mostly of two gases, hydrogen and helium, and it has no solid ground to stand on. Kit looked at the churning surface and was glad that the Skylift was only imagined.

The centre of the Sun is about 15 million degrees Celsius, and there the pressure is huge. Hydrogen atoms are squeezed together to make helium, and this is called fusion, which gives out energy as light and heat.
The light made in the Sun's core cannot fly straight out, because the gas is so thick. It bumps from atom to atom, and it takes many thousands of years just to reach the surface.
The surface of the Sun is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, which is hot enough to melt any metal. Sunspots are dark patches that look black only because they are cooler than the gas around them.

Around the Sun lies a thin, pale glow called the corona, which we can see during a total eclipse. Strangely, it is hotter than the surface, at more than a million degrees, and scientists are still working out why.
The Sun sends out a stream of particles called the solar wind. In 2021 a spacecraft named the Parker Solar Probe flew into the corona, the first to touch the Sun's atmosphere.
The Sun is about four and a half billion years old, and it has about as long to go. Plants use its light to grow, animals eat plants, and so almost all life on Earth runs on sunlight.
Beyond the Moon lie the four rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. They are small and solid, and like all the planets they circle the Sun in the same direction.

Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, and it races around it in only 88 days. It has almost no air, so its days are scorching, at about 430 degrees Celsius, and its nights are freezing.
Strangely, spacecraft have found ice on Mercury, the planet nearest the Sun. It hides in deep craters near the poles, where the Sun never shines and the temperature stays far below freezing.
Venus is wrapped in thick clouds, and its air is mostly carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat. The ground is about 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, so Venus is hotter than Mercury.
Venus turns very slowly, and in the opposite direction to most planets. One day there lasts about 243 Earth days, which is longer than its year of about 225 days.
Mars is about half as wide as Earth, and it is red because its dust contains rusted iron. Its air is thin and mostly carbon dioxide, and strangely, its sunsets are blue.

Mars has a giant volcano, Olympus Mons, which is about 22 kilometres high, about two and a half times taller than Mount Everest. It also has a canyon called Valles Marineris, about 4,000 kilometres long.

Mars has dry riverbeds and old lake beds, so water must once have flowed over its surface. In 2021 a robot named Perseverance landed in a crater that was once a lake, to search for signs of ancient life.

Perseverance carried a tiny helicopter called Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet in April 2021. Flying is hard on Mars because the air is so thin, so its blades had to spin very fast.
Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos, which are lumpy and shaped like potatoes. Phobos is only about 22 kilometres across, and it circles Mars three times a day.
Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, a wide ring of rocks left over from when the planets were formed. All its rocks together weigh less than the Moon, and it is mostly empty space.

Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt, about 940 kilometres across, and it is round like a small planet. It is called a dwarf planet, and a spacecraft named Dawn found strange bright spots on its surface.
Most asteroids are not solid mountains but loose piles of rubble held together by their own weak gravity. Some even have tiny moons, which circle them as the Moon circles Earth.

Spacecraft have visited asteroids and brought back samples of them. Japan's Hayabusa2 returned dust from an asteroid called Ryugu in 2020, and the American OSIRIS-REx returned dust from Bennu in 2023.
Kit saw a bright streak in the sky far below. A shooting star is only a tiny grain of dust burning up in the air, and it is called a meteor.
Most space rocks burn up, but some are big enough to reach the ground, and these are called meteorites. Some are mostly iron, and the oldest are about four and a half billion years old.
About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about ten kilometres wide struck Earth near what is now Mexico. It left a crater called Chicxulub, and soon after, most of the dinosaurs died.
Dust and smoke blocked the sunlight for a long time, and the world became cold and dark. Most big animals died, yet small ones survived, and birds are descendants of dinosaurs that lived through it.

Today, astronomers use telescopes to find the asteroids that pass near Earth, and they have found many thousands. None of the large ones that we know about is likely to hit us for at least a hundred years.
In 2022 a spacecraft called DART crashed on purpose into Dimorphos, a small moon of an asteroid. It changed the moon's orbit by about half an hour, which proved that we could move an asteroid.
Jupiter is by far the biggest planet, about eleven times wider than Earth. More than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it, and it weighs more than twice as much as all the other planets together.
