Above him, even though the Sun was shining, the sky was as black as midnight.

Kit noticed a line of boot prints pressed into the dust, sharp and clear as if they had been made yesterday. They were left by the Apollo astronauts, twelve of whom walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, and no wind or rain has touched them since. Noor said they may last for millions of years, wearing away only very slowly.

Gravity, the pull that every object has on every other object, depends on how much matter there is, and the Moon has far less than Earth. Its pull is only about one sixth as strong, so Kit gave a small hop and sailed upwards much higher than he had ever jumped before. He came down slowly, laughing, like a feather drifting through a still room, and he could not stop grinning.

Everywhere Kit looked, the ground was pitted with round craters, from tiny dents no bigger than a coin to basins hundreds of kilometres wide. Each one is the scar of a space rock that struck the surface at enormous speed. With no air to slow the rocks and no weather to smooth the scars, the Moon keeps a record of its past that goes back billions of years.

The dark patches that people have long imagined as a face are in fact vast plains of dark rock, formed when lava flooded old basins billions of years ago. Because the Moon turns exactly once in the time that it takes to circle Earth, we always see the same side. The far side, which was first photographed in 1959, has many more craters and far fewer of these dark plains.

The Moon makes no light of its own, and it glows only because it reflects the light of the Sun. As it travels around Earth, we see its sunlit half from a changing angle, so it seems to swell from a thin crescent to a full circle and then shrink away again. This cycle repeats about every month, and it has been used to measure time for thousands of years.

The Moon's gravity tugs gently on Earth, and the oceans, which are free to flow, rise into a bulge on the side nearest to it. A second bulge forms on the opposite side, so as the planet turns, most coasts have two high tides and two low tides each day. Noor said that fishing people and sailors have lived by this rhythm for as long as there have been boats.

Noor pointed out a remarkable coincidence: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also about 400 times further away. The two therefore look almost exactly the same size in our sky, and now and then the Moon slides across the Sun and hides it completely. During a total eclipse, the day turns dark, the birds go quiet and the Sun's pale outer glow becomes visible.

Noor said that the best idea we have is that, about four and a half billion years ago, a body about the size of Mars crashed into the young Earth. The cloud of molten rock thrown into orbit slowly gathered together under its own gravity and became the Moon. It is still drifting away from us today, at about the speed that a fingernail grows.

Noor explained that light travels at about 300,000 kilometres every second, a speed that nothing in the universe can beat. In a single second, a beam of light could circle the Earth more than seven times. It is so fast that, in everyday life, we simply see things the instant they happen.

The Skylift sped on towards the Sun, which lies about 150 million kilometres from Earth, a distance that even light needs about eight minutes to cross. Noor said that if the Sun were to vanish suddenly, we would go on enjoying its light and its pull for eight whole minutes. Then the daylight would fade, Earth would drift off in a straight line, and nobody would have had any warning.

Kit stared at the Sun, which is an ordinary star but looks enormous up close, about 109 times wider than Earth. More than a million planets the size of ours could be packed inside it with room to spare. The Sun contains more than 99 percent of all the mass in the Solar System, and the planets are only leftovers.

Noor told him that the Sun is made mostly of the two lightest gases, hydrogen and helium, and that it has no solid ground at all. The surface that we see is simply the layer of gas where the light finally escapes into space. Kit looked at the boiling, churning glow and was very glad that the Skylift was only imagined.

Deep in the Sun's core, the temperature is about 15 million degrees Celsius, and the weight of the gas above presses down with enormous force. Under such conditions, hydrogen atoms are forced together to form helium in a process called fusion. Each second, the Sun turns about four million tonnes of matter into energy, and it has been doing so for billions of years.

The Sun's gas is so dense that light made in the core cannot travel straight out. It bounces from one particle to the next, wandering this way and that, and estimates say that the journey to the surface takes many thousands of years. After that, the final trip to Earth takes only eight minutes, so the sunlight on Kit's face was truly ancient.

The visible surface of the Sun measures about 5,500 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt any metal we know. Here and there, dark blemishes called sunspots appear on its surface, drifting slowly across the face of the star. They look black only by comparison, for they are cooler than the glowing gas around them, and they come and go in a rhythm of about eleven years.

During a total eclipse, a pale halo appears around the black disc of the Moon, and this is the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona. Strangely, it is hundreds of times hotter than the surface beneath it, reaching more than a million degrees. Noor admitted that this is a real puzzle, and that scientists are still working out exactly how the Sun heats it.

Beyond the Sun's surface streams the solar wind, a constant flow of particles that blows out past all the planets. In 2021 a spacecraft called the Parker Solar Probe became the first to fly through the corona, close enough to taste the Sun's atmosphere. It survives by hiding behind a heat shield, which stays hot while the machinery behind it is kept cool.

Noor said that the Sun is about four and a half billion years old, which is roughly halfway through its life as a steady star. Every green leaf on Earth catches its light and turns it into food, and nearly every animal depends on those plants, directly or not. Kit realised that the energy in his breakfast had once been sunshine falling on a field.

Noor swept her hand across the window to show the four inner planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. They are small, dense worlds of rock and metal with solid surfaces you could stand on. Like all the planets, they travel around the Sun in the same direction, along paths that lie almost in a single flat sheet.

Mercury, the smallest planet, lies only about 58 million kilometres from the Sun and completes a lap of it in just 88 days. Because it has almost no air to hold the heat, its sunlit side reaches about 430 degrees Celsius, while the night side falls to about minus 180. It is a world of extremes, and its whole surface is scarred with craters like those of the Moon.

In one of nature's odd surprises, a spacecraft has found water ice on Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun. It lies hidden inside deep craters near the poles, where sunlight never reaches the floor and the cold never lifts. Noor smiled and said that the universe seems to love proving our expectations wrong, and that this is exactly why we go and look.

Thick clouds, partly made of sulphuric acid, hide the surface of Venus from view completely and for ever. Its heavy air is mostly carbon dioxide, which traps heat like a blanket, and so the ground is about 465 degrees Celsius. That is hot enough to melt lead, and it makes Venus hotter than Mercury even though it is much further from the Sun.

Venus spins slowly and in the opposite direction to most other planets, so on its surface the Sun would rise in the west. A single turn takes about 243 Earth days, which is longer than the 225 days it needs to go around the Sun. Astronomers do not yet agree on exactly why it spins this way, though a great collision long ago is one idea.

Mars is about half as wide as Earth, and its red colour comes from iron in the dust that has rusted over billions of years. The air is thin and cold, far too thin for us to breathe, and the sky above the plains is a dusty pink. Noor added that, oddly enough, Martian sunsets glow a cool blue, because the fine dust scatters the light in an unusual way.

On Mars, the volcano Olympus Mons rises about 22 kilometres above the plain, which makes it about two and a half times higher than Mount Everest. Across the planet, a scar called Valles Marineris stretches about 4,000 kilometres, long enough to reach across most of the United States. Everything on Mars seems to have been built on a truly grand scale, as if the planet were showing off.

Long ago, Mars was warmer and wetter, and rivers ran across its surface into lakes. In 2021 a robot rover named Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, which was once the site of one such lake, and began to search the rocks for signs of ancient life. So far, nobody has found proof that life ever existed on Mars, but the search goes on.

Tucked under the belly of Perseverance was a tiny helicopter named Ingenuity, which made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet in April 2021. The air on Mars is about one hundredth as thick as ours, so the helicopter's blades had to spin much faster than those of a helicopter on Earth. It was built for a few test flights, yet it kept flying for nearly three years.

Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, each shaped more like a lumpy potato than a ball. Phobos is only about 22 kilometres across and circles Mars about three times a day, close enough that its orbit is slowly shrinking. Noor said it may break apart in tens of millions of years, and then, as the lift rose again, they left the rocky planets behind.

Between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, the Skylift entered the asteroid belt, a broad ring of rocky leftovers from the birth of the Solar System. Jupiter's strong gravity stirred these rocks so violently that they never joined together into a planet. All of them added up would weigh less than our Moon, so the belt is mostly empty space and spacecraft cross it safely.

Ceres, the largest object in the belt, measures about 940 kilometres across and is massive enough to have pulled itself into a ball. For this reason it is called a dwarf planet rather than an asteroid, a name it shares with Pluto. The spacecraft Dawn orbited it in 2015 and found curious bright spots, which turned out to be patches of salt left behind by water.

Most asteroids, Noor said, are not solid mountains but heaps of rubble, boulders and dust held together by their own feeble gravity. Some are shaped like spinning tops, and some are even accompanied by tiny moons. They look battered and ordinary, yet they preserve material that has barely changed since the Solar System began.

Rather than guess what asteroids are made of, scientists have gone to fetch some. The Japanese spacecraft Hayabusa2 returned a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in 2020, and the American spacecraft OSIRIS-REx did the same from Bennu in 2023. Both samples are rich in carbon, and researchers are studying them for clues about the ingredients that once built the planets.

Far below the lift, a bright streak raced across the dark sky and vanished. Noor explained that a shooting star is not a star at all but a grain of rock or dust, often no bigger than a grain of sand, which glows as it rushes through the air at tremendous speed. We call it a meteor, and Earth meets huge numbers of them every night, most of them too faint to see.

Most meteors burn up completely, but now and then a stone survives its fall and lands, and then it is called a meteorite. Some are mostly iron, others mostly rock, and the oldest are about four and a half billion years old. By measuring their age, scientists have worked out when the Solar System first formed.

Noor took Kit back in time to a day about 66 million years ago, when an asteroid roughly ten kilometres wide crashed into the sea near what is now Mexico. The impact dug a crater called Chicxulub, more than 150 kilometres across, and threw dust and fire high above the planet. It was one of the worst days that life on Earth has ever endured.

The dust and smoke in the sky blocked out the sunlight, and plants failed and food chains collapsed. About three quarters of all species disappeared, including all of the large dinosaurs that had ruled the land for millions of years. Yet small animals, many of them furry, found shelter and survived, and birds, which are living descendants of the dinosaurs, still sing in our gardens today.

Today astronomers search the sky for asteroids that cross Earth's path, and they have already found tens of thousands of them. None of the big ones that we know about is expected to hit us for at least the next hundred years. The aim is to find any dangerous rock early, because an early warning gives us time to act.

In September 2022, a spacecraft named DART flew deliberately into Dimorphos, a small asteroid that circles a larger one, to test whether a collision could change its path. The orbit of Dimorphos became shorter by about half an hour, a result that astonished the scientists. For the first time, humans had changed the motion of a natural object in space, and Kit scribbled the date in his notebook.

Jupiter filled the whole window of the Skylift, the undisputed king of the planets, about eleven times wider than Earth. More than 1,300 Earths could be packed inside it, and it holds more than twice as much matter as all of the other planets added together. Kit felt like an ant looking up at a mountain, and he wrote the word enormous three times in his notebook.

Noor said that Jupiter is a gas giant, made mostly of the same hydrogen and helium as the Sun, with no solid surface to land on. It spins faster than any other planet, completing a full turn in less than ten hours, and that rapid rotation stretches its clouds into bright and dark bands. Powerful winds blow along these bands in opposite directions, and they never seem to tire.

Kit pointed at a vast red oval that swirled in the clouds, which Noor called the Great Red Spot. This storm is wider than our whole planet, with winds of several hundred kilometres an hour, and astronomers have watched it for at least 150 years. It has been slowly shrinking, though, and nobody can say for certain how long it will last.

Since 2016, a solar-powered spacecraft called Juno has swung around Jupiter in long loops, peering beneath the clouds with its instruments. It has found clusters of enormous storms spinning at both poles, and it has measured the planet's gravity and magnetic field with great care. Deep down, the pressure is so great that hydrogen is squeezed into a strange liquid, which is another reason that nobody could ever stand on Jupiter.

In January 1610, the Italian scientist Galileo turned a new telescope towards Jupiter and noticed four tiny points of light lined up beside it. Night after night they changed places, and he realised that they were moons circling Jupiter. This was important evidence that not everything in the sky goes around the Earth, and Jupiter now has nearly a hundred known moons.

Io, the innermost of the four large moons, is the most volcanic place in the whole Solar System, with hundreds of volcanoes that spout fountains of lava and gas. Jupiter's gravity squeezes and stretches the moon as it orbits, and the friction inside heats the rock until it melts. The yellow, orange and red tints on its surface come mostly from sulphur, which makes Io look like an unbaked pizza.

Europa, a little smaller than our Moon, has a smooth, cracked shell of ice, and beneath it lies a deep ocean of salty water. Scientists think this ocean may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's seas put together, and the spacecraft Europa Clipper is on its way to study it. Whether anything swims in that dark water is one of the great open questions of astronomy.

Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger even than the planet Mercury, although it weighs only about half as much because it is made partly of ice. It is the only moon known to produce its own magnetic field, like a small planet of its own. Further out, the moon Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered places anywhere, its dark surface unchanged for billions of years.

In July 1994, the broken fragments of a comet called Shoemaker-Levy 9 slammed one after another into Jupiter, and astronomers around the world watched. It was the first time that anyone had seen a collision between two bodies in the Solar System, and the impacts left dark scars in the clouds, some of them as big as Earth. The marks faded within months, but the lesson remained: space is still an active place.

Jupiter has the strongest magnetic field of any planet, a vast invisible bubble that traps energetic particles and fills the space around it with dangerous radiation. At its poles, glowing auroras shine far brighter and larger than anything on Earth, and they ripple in ultraviolet light. Noor gently suggested that, even in imagination, it was wise to leave before the radiation became a problem, and the lift swung away towards the next planet.

Saturn, the second largest planet, is about nine times wider than Earth, yet it is so light that its average density is lower than that of water. Noor joked that if anyone could build a bath big enough, Saturn would bob on the surface like a rubber duck. Its soft yellow clouds are mostly hydrogen and helium, just like those of Jupiter.

Kit pressed his face to the glass as the rings came into view, a great wheel of shining ice made from billions of separate pieces. Some are no bigger than grains of sugar, and others are as large as houses, and every one of them is orbiting Saturn in its own path. The rings stretch for hundreds of thousands of kilometres, yet in most places they are astonishingly thin, only about ten metres from top to bottom.

When Galileo first looked at Saturn, his small telescope showed him only a blurred planet with strange lumps on either side, which he thought were ears or companions. It took until 1655 for the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens, with a better telescope, to explain that these shapes were really a flat ring around the planet. Today, astronomers still argue about whether the rings are young or very old, and the question is far from settled.

Cassini reached Saturn in 2004 and spent thirteen years sending back thousands of pictures and measurements of the planet, its rings and its many moons. When its fuel was nearly gone, controllers steered it into Saturn's atmosphere in 2017, where it burned up. They did this deliberately, so that the craft could never crash into a moon and carry Earth's germs to a place where something might be alive.

Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, is wrapped in a thick orange haze, and its air is denser than Earth's. On its surface, rivers and lakes are filled not with water but with liquid methane and ethane, which would be natural gas on Earth. In 2005 the probe Huygens parachuted down through the haze and landed there, the most distant landing ever made at that time.

Enceladus is only about 500 kilometres wide, but it is one of the most interesting places in the Solar System. From long cracks near its south pole, fountains of water vapour and ice grains spray out into space, and Cassini flew through them to taste what they contained. They come from a salty ocean hidden under the ice, and the water holds some of the ingredients that life needs.

Uranus was discovered in 1781 by William Herschel, who at first believed he had found a comet, and it was the first planet that nobody had known about since ancient times. It is a pale blue-green world, coloured by methane in its air, and it rolls around the Sun tipped almost on its side. As a result each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of darkness.

No spacecraft has ever orbited Uranus or Neptune, and only one has even passed them. Voyager 2 flew by Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, and the pictures it sent home remain the main close views that we have of both worlds. Noor said that scientists dream of going back, because each of these ice giants still holds many secrets.

Neptune is a deep blue world where the winds reach about 2,000 kilometres an hour, faster than any other planet. It was found in 1846 when mathematicians calculated where an unseen planet must be, to explain the odd motion of Uranus, and astronomers found it just where the sums predicted. Sunlight takes about four hours to reach it, and a single Neptune year lasts 165 Earth years.

Neptune's largest moon, Triton, travels around the planet in the wrong direction, a strong sign that it did not form there. Most astronomers think it was a free-roaming icy world, perhaps from the far edge of the Solar System, which was captured by Neptune's gravity long ago. Voyager 2 saw plumes of dark material rising from its frozen surface, and the Sun by now looked like only a very bright star.

Beyond Neptune, the lift reached Pluto, a small and frozen world that an American astronomer named Clyde Tombaugh discovered in 1930. It is smaller than our own Moon, and it takes 248 Earth years to travel once around the Sun. Sunlight there is so faint that noon on Pluto is about as bright as twilight on Earth.

In 2006 the International Astronomical Union agreed on a definition of a planet, and Pluto no longer qualified. A planet must orbit the Sun, be round, and have cleared its neighbourhood of other large objects, whereas Pluto shares its crowded region with many similar icy worlds. Kit looked a little sad, but Noor said Pluto was the same fascinating place it had always been, whatever name we gave it.

It took the spacecraft New Horizons nine and a half years to reach Pluto, and in July 2015 it swept past at tremendous speed, taking pictures for only a few hours. The images astonished everyone: Pluto had mountains of water ice, a thin blue haze in its sky, and a vast heart-shaped plain of frozen gas. Scientists had expected a dead, dull ball, but they found a world full of surprises.

Charon is Pluto's largest moon, and it is so big, about half the width of Pluto itself, that the two worlds circle a point in the empty space between them. Astronomers sometimes call them a double world rather than a planet and its moon. They also keep the same faces towards each other, so each would hang motionless in the other's sky.

Pluto is only one member of the Kuiper belt, a vast, doughnut-shaped region beyond Neptune that holds thousands of known icy worlds and probably many more. After Pluto, New Horizons flew past a small member of this crowd, named Arrokoth, on the first day of 2019. It turned out to be shaped like a snowman, formed when two round lumps touched gently and stuck together.

A comet is a lump of ice, dust and frozen gas, usually only a few kilometres across, that has been described as a dirty snowball. As it nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas and releases dust, forming a glowing cloud and a tail that stretches for millions of kilometres. The tail always points away from the Sun, pushed outwards by sunlight and the solar wind, even when the comet is leaving.

In 1705, the English astronomer Edmond Halley realised that comets which people had recorded in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were all one object, returning every 76 years or so. He predicted its return in 1758, and when it appeared on time, after his death, the comet was named in his honour. It was last seen in 1986, and it should light up the sky again in 2061.

The European spacecraft Rosetta travelled for ten years to reach a comet in 2014, and then it circled it for two more, watching it closely. In November 2014 it released a small lander named Philae, the first machine ever to land on a comet, though it bounced twice and came to rest in the shadow of a cliff. Rosetta showed that the comet is shaped like a rubber duck, made of two lumps joined together.

Astronomers believe that far beyond the Kuiper belt lies the Oort cloud, a huge, spherical shell of frozen rocks that surrounds the whole Solar System. Nobody has seen it directly, because its members are too small and faint, but it would explain why some comets arrive from every direction and take thousands of years to come back. Its outer edge may be about a light-year or more from the Sun, so it is almost beyond imagining.

The solar wind blows outwards until it meets the thin gas between the stars, and there it forms the edge of a huge bubble called the heliosphere. This boundary lies roughly four times as far from the Sun as Neptune does, and in 2012 the spacecraft Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to cross it. Noor said that the Skylift was now leaving the Sun's own territory and entering the great gap between the stars.

A tiny spacecraft with a dish and long arms drifted past the window, and Noor introduced it as Voyager 1. Launched in 1977, it travels at about 17 kilometres every second and is now the most distant object that people have ever made. Its radio signals, even at the speed of light, need nearly a day to reach Earth.

Fixed to the side of Voyager is a gold-plated copy of a record, made as a message in a bottle for any being that might one day find it. It holds greetings in 55 languages, music from many cultures, the songs of whales, the sound of a kiss and 115 pictures of life on our planet. The chance of anyone finding it is tiny, but it may survive for a billion years or more.

In 1990, when Voyager 1 was about six billion kilometres from home, scientists asked it to turn around and photograph the planets behind it. In one picture, Earth is just a pale blue dot, less than a single pixel wide, caught in a beam of scattered sunlight. Everyone who has ever lived, Noor said quietly, lived on that speck, and so did all of their joys and troubles.

Because the distances between stars are so enormous, astronomers measure them in light-years, which is the distance that light travels in one year. That is about nine and a half trillion kilometres, a number so large that it is easier to picture as a journey of time. When we say a star is four light-years away, we mean that its light needed four years to reach us.

The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, which lies about four light-years away, or roughly 40 trillion kilometres. It is a small, cool, red star so dim that nobody can see it without a telescope, and it belongs to a family of three stars known as Alpha Centauri. Even this closest neighbour, Noor said, is a vast distance beyond the Solar System.

Noor offered Kit a way to picture the emptiness between the stars, using only a piece of fruit. Imagine that the Sun is a grapefruit sitting on a table in London, she said, and Earth is a speck of dust about ten metres away. The next star, Proxima Centauri, would then be another small fruit about 3,000 kilometres away, roughly as far as Turkey, with almost nothing in between.

Kit asked how long it would take to reach even the nearest star, and Noor did the sums. At the speed of Voyager 1, one of the fastest craft ever built, the journey to Proxima Centauri would last about 75,000 years, far longer than the whole of written history. This is why the Skylift, which exists only in imagination, is the only vehicle that can make this tour in a single night.

On a clear, dark night, a person with good eyes can see about 5,000 stars in the whole sky, though only part of the sky is visible at once. The brightest of them is Sirius, about nine light-years away, so the light that reaches us tonight left it nine years ago. Every star we see is therefore a window into the past, shown as it was when its light set out.

Look carefully, Noor said, and you will notice that stars are not all white but have faint tints of blue, yellow, orange and red. The colour is a clue to the temperature, just as the glow of a metal poker changes as it is heated, so that blue stars are the hottest and red stars the coolest. Our Sun, a yellow star with a surface of about 5,500 degrees, lies somewhere in the middle.

In the constellation of Orion, the hunter's shoulder is marked by Betelgeuse, a red supergiant so vast that if it stood where the Sun does, it would swallow the planets as far out as Mars and beyond. It is also a reminder that the shapes we call constellations are only chance patterns, because the stars in them lie at very different distances from us. Noor said that it was time to go and see where stars actually come from.

Ahead of the Skylift glowed a vast cloud of pink, blue and violet gas, which Noor named the Orion Nebula. About 1,350 light-years from Earth, it is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye as a faint fuzzy patch in Orion's sword. Clouds like this one, made mostly of hydrogen and dust, are the nurseries where new stars are born.

Inside the cloud, the gas is not perfectly smooth, and gravity draws the denser clumps in on themselves. As a clump contracts, the gas falls inwards and heats up, until it glows as a young object called a protostar. This stage can last many thousands of years, and all the while the baby star is hidden from sight by the dust around it.

When the heart of a protostar becomes hot enough, at about ten million degrees, hydrogen atoms begin to fuse into helium, and an immense amount of energy is released. The outward push of this heat balances the inward pull of gravity, so the star stops shrinking and settles into a steady life. It is at this moment, Noor said, that a star is truly born, and the nebula begins to glow around it.

Before them rose the Pillars of Creation, towering columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, made famous by the Hubble Space Telescope in 1995. Each column is several light-years tall, and new stars are forming at their tips and inside them. In 2022 the Webb Space Telescope photographed them again in infrared light, which can see through some of the dust.

Stars are rarely born alone, for a single cloud makes hundreds or thousands of them at once. The Pleiades, a cluster you can see with your own eyes, is a young group of stars about 440 light-years away, perhaps only a hundred million years old. The Sun almost certainly began in a crowd like this, though its siblings have long since drifted far apart.

Around a young star, the cloud's leftover gas and dust flatten into a spinning disc, and in it, tiny grains stick together to form pebbles. Pebbles gather into rocks, rocks collide and merge, and over millions of years the largest of them become planets. Our own Solar System formed in this way about four and a half billion years ago, and telescopes have photographed other discs with gaps where young planets are clearing their paths.

Close to a young star, the heat drives off the light gases and ice, leaving only rock and metal to build small planets like Mercury and Earth. Farther out, past a point called the frost line, ice survives, and the planets that grow there can become huge enough to capture great amounts of gas. This is why the Solar System has small rocky planets near the Sun and giants in the cold outer parts.

Planets that circle other stars are called exoplanets, and for most of history nobody knew whether they existed. In 1995 two Swiss astronomers found the first one around a Sun-like star, called 51 Pegasi b, and they later shared a Nobel Prize for it. Since then, thousands more have been found, which shows that planets are very common in our galaxy.

Exoplanets are far too faint to see directly in most cases, so astronomers watch the star instead. When a planet crosses in front of it, the star dims by a tiny fraction, and space telescopes such as Kepler and TESS can measure that change precisely. Kepler alone found thousands of planets, and it showed that the typical star probably has at least one.

In the TRAPPIST-1 system, about 40 light-years away, seven planets roughly the size of Earth circle a small, cool red star, all of them closer to it than Mercury is to our Sun. Several lie in the habitable zone, where the temperature could allow liquid water, and the Webb telescope is studying their air. We do not yet know whether life exists anywhere beyond Earth, and Noor said that this is one of the greatest questions of our time.

Noor explained that most stars, the Sun included, spend the great majority of their lives quietly fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. Strangely, the heavier a star is, the shorter its life, because its enormous weight squeezes the core so hard that it burns its fuel at a ferocious rate. A star is like a bank account, she said: the richest are often the quickest to spend.

Red dwarfs are small, cool stars, and they are by far the most common kind in our galaxy, making up about three quarters of all stars. They sip their fuel so sparingly that they can shine for trillions of years, which is hundreds of times longer than the present age of the universe. Not one red dwarf has yet had time to die, and the first of them is still young.

At the other extreme are the giant blue stars, many times heavier than the Sun and thousands of times brighter. They live fast and die young, lasting only a few million years before their fuel runs out, which in cosmic terms is no more than the blink of an eye. By comparison, the Sun's ten-billion-year life seems calm, sensible and almost a little dull to a giant of that kind.

The Sun has enough hydrogen left to shine steadily for about another five billion years. When the core runs out, the outer layers will swell into a red giant that engulfs Mercury and Venus, and perhaps Earth as well, though scientists are not sure about that. Long before that, in about a billion years, the Sun will have grown so bright that Earth's oceans will begin to boil away.

When its fuel is finally gone, the Sun will puff its outer layers into space, forming a glowing shell of gas called a planetary nebula, which has nothing to do with planets. At the centre will remain a white dwarf, the core of the old star, squeezed to about the size of Earth. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about five tonnes, and it will fade very slowly over trillions of years.

In stars at least eight times heavier than the Sun, the core grows hot enough to fuse helium into carbon, then oxygen, and on through heavier atoms in a series of shells, like the layers of an onion. At last the core turns to iron, and here the process stops, because fusing iron takes in energy instead of giving it out. Without its source of heat to hold it up, the core collapses in less than a second.

The collapse of the core releases a wave of energy that blasts the star's outer layers into space in an explosion called a supernova. For a few weeks, a single supernova can shine as brightly as an entire galaxy of billions of stars. In 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded one so bright that it was visible in daylight, and its remains are still glowing today as the Crab Nebula.

At the beginning, the universe contained almost nothing but hydrogen and helium, so every other ingredient had to be made by stars. Carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, iron and many more were cooked in their cores, and when stars die, they scatter these atoms into space. Later generations of stars and planets are built from the ashes of earlier ones, which is exactly how Earth came to exist.

Even supernovae cannot make everything, and many of the heaviest elements, such as gold and platinum, seem to be forged when two dead stars called neutron stars collide. Astronomers saw such a crash in 2017, when they detected both a bright flash and the ripples in space that it sent out. Noor smiled and said that every gold ring in the world is therefore a souvenir of a collision between stars.

Noor told Kit that nearly all the atoms in his body, except hydrogen, which dates from the Big Bang, were forged inside stars that died long before the Sun was born. The calcium in his bones, the iron in his blood and the oxygen in every breath were all made in those far-off furnaces. Kit held up his hand against the glittering sky, and for the first time he felt that he and the stars were made of the same stuff.

After a supernova, the core of the star may be crushed into a neutron star, a ball only about 20 kilometres across but heavier than the whole Sun. Gravity squeezes it so hard that atoms collapse, and the matter inside is made almost entirely of neutrons packed tightly together. A single teaspoon of this material would weigh billions of tonnes, more than all the people on Earth.

Some neutron stars spin rapidly and send beams of radio waves out from their magnetic poles, so that a beam sweeps past Earth like the light of a lighthouse. We detect it as a regular pulse, and the fastest of these pulsars turn hundreds of times every second. When the first one was found in 1967, the signal was so steady that astronomers wondered for a moment whether it came from an alien civilisation.

For the heaviest stars, even the stiffness of neutrons cannot hold the core up, and the collapse goes on without end. What is left is a black hole, a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can get out. The boundary of this region is called the event horizon, and once anything crosses it, there is no way back.

Light is the fastest thing in the universe, so if even light cannot escape from a black hole, nothing can. Kit looked at the black sphere ahead and saw that the stars behind it were bent and smeared into rings, as if seen through thick glass. Noor reminded him that this happens because gravity itself bends the path of light, a fact first predicted by Albert Einstein.

It is a common mistake to imagine black holes as cosmic vacuum cleaners, dragging in everything within reach. If the Sun were replaced overnight by a black hole of the same mass, the planets would continue in the same orbits, and the real change would be that the sky would go dark and Earth would freeze. Gravity is dangerous only for those who stray too close to the horizon, which is exactly why Noor kept the lift well back.

Einstein showed that gravity slows time, so a clock close to a black hole would tick far more slowly than one on Earth, and a traveller watching from far away would see it almost stop. Close to a small black hole, the pull on your feet would be much greater than the pull on your head, which would stretch you out like spaghetti. Noor assured Kit that the Skylift, being imaginary, would keep a very polite distance from any such place.

Because a black hole gives out no light, astronomers find them by their effects on their surroundings. Gas that spirals towards one is heated to millions of degrees and shines brightly in X-rays, which is how the black hole in the system Cygnus X-1, about 6,000 light-years away, was first identified. Other black holes reveal themselves by the way they make nearby stars swing around them.

Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916, but it took a century before anyone could detect them. In September 2015 the LIGO detectors recorded a tiny ripple in space that had been made by two black holes merging more than a billion light-years away. The ripple changed the length of the detectors' long arms by less than the width of a proton, yet it opened a new way of listening to the universe.

In April 2019, a team of astronomers who had linked radio telescopes across the whole Earth released the first ever image of a black hole. It shows a dark shadow surrounded by a glowing ring of hot gas, and the object at its heart, in the galaxy M87, weighs about six and a half billion times as much as the Sun. A similar picture of the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy followed in 2022.

Black holes come in many sizes, and those made by dying stars weigh only a few times as much as the Sun. Our galaxy may contain as many as a hundred million of them, while the supermassive kind weigh millions or even billions of Suns. Nearly every large galaxy seems to have one at its centre, and Noor said that our own galaxy is no exception.

The lift climbed above the plane of our galaxy until the whole Milky Way spread out beneath them like a glowing wheel. It is about 100,000 light-years across, and it contains hundreds of billions of stars, most of them with planets of their own. Kit realised that every star he had ever seen at night belonged to just this one island in the dark.

Noor pointed to a tiny glimmer on a faint arm of the spiral and said that this was home. The Sun lies about 26,000 light-years from the centre, roughly halfway out to the edge, in a quiet district rather than a crowded one. Astronomers think this calm position may be lucky for life, because there are fewer violent explosions nearby.

The Sun and all its planets circle the centre of the galaxy at about 220 kilometres every second, a speed that is hard to imagine. Even so, a single lap takes about 230 million years, which means the Sun has completed only about twenty laps since it was born. The last time that we were in this spot of the galaxy, Noor said, the first dinosaurs were just beginning to appear.

Because we live inside the disc of the galaxy, we see the Milky Way from the side, as a pale river of light that crosses the night sky. The ancient Greeks called it the milky circle, and many cultures have told stories about it. In 1610 Galileo pointed his telescope at it and discovered that the glow is really the light of countless stars too faint to see one by one.

Kit took out his notebook and asked how long it would take to count all the stars in the galaxy. Noor worked it out: at one star every second, without stopping to eat or sleep, counting a hundred billion stars would take more than 3,000 years. That is only one galaxy, she added, and there are hundreds of billions of galaxies still to come.

Seen from above, the Milky Way is a barred spiral, with a long bar of stars across its middle and graceful arms curling outwards. Its disc is astonishingly thin, only about a thousand light-years thick in comparison with a width of 100,000, so that it is proportioned like a pancake. Surrounding the whole disc is a faint, spherical halo of old stars, which stretches far beyond the visible spiral.

Orbiting high above the disc are about 150 globular clusters, dense balls that pack hundreds of thousands of stars into a space only a few dozen light-years wide. Their stars are very old, in some cases more than ten billion years, so these clusters are like fossils from the early days of the galaxy. They are among the oldest objects in the galaxy, and each one is a tight swarm held together by its own gravity.

At the very centre of our galaxy lies a giant black hole named Sagittarius A star, about four million times as heavy as the Sun. Astronomers tracked the stars that race around it for decades, and one of them completes an orbit every sixteen years, moving at a few percent of the speed of light. This work earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for two of the teams involved.

The European space telescope Gaia, launched in 2013, has measured the exact positions and movements of nearly two billion stars, which is about one in a hundred of those in the galaxy. From these measurements, astronomers are building a three-dimensional map of the Milky Way and learning how it grew by swallowing smaller galaxies. It is the most detailed star map in history, and it keeps growing as new data arrive.

Two small neighbouring galaxies, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, orbit the Milky Way at distances of about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years. People in the southern half of the world can see them with the naked eye as faint, detached clouds in the night sky. They are just the nearest of many neighbours, Noor said, and the largest of them lay much farther away.

The Skylift left the Milky Way behind and began to cross the great emptiness between galaxies, a gap so wide that light itself needs millions of years to cross it. Ahead glowed the Andromeda galaxy, which lies about two and a half million light-years away from the Milky Way. It is the farthest thing that most people can see with the naked eye, a faint smudge of light that left its home before humans existed.

Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own, although it is somewhat bigger, with about a trillion stars. On a clear, dark night, you can find it as a faint oval smudge high in the northern autumn sky, and the light you see left it about two and a half million years ago. Noor said that one day Kit should look at it and remember that he had visited.

Barely a century ago, many astronomers believed that the Milky Way was the entire universe, and that fuzzy patches like Andromeda were clouds of gas inside it. In 1924 Edwin Hubble settled the argument when he measured the distance to Andromeda and found that it was far too great for it to belong to our galaxy. Almost overnight, the known universe became far larger than anyone had imagined, and it has kept growing ever since.

Hubble's measurement depended on the work of Henrietta Leavitt, who around 1912 studied stars called Cepheids that brighten and fade in a regular rhythm. She discovered that the slower such a star pulses, the more powerful it really is, so by comparing its true brightness with how bright it looks, astronomers can work out its distance. A star of known brightness is like a lamp of known power, and it tells you how far off it stands.

Andromeda is not at rest but falling towards the Milky Way at about 110 kilometres every second. Astronomers once believed that the two galaxies would collide in about four or five billion years, although newer measurements suggest that this is less certain than we thought. If they do merge, the combined galaxy has already been given a nickname: Milkomeda.

When galaxies merge, their stars very rarely collide, because the gaps between them are enormous compared with the sizes of the stars themselves. It would be like two swarms of bees passing through each other in a vast empty hall, with hardly any bumps. The result is a new, rounder galaxy, and the night sky of any planet inside it would change completely over millions of years.

Galaxies come in three main shapes, which astronomers call spiral, elliptical and irregular, and all three are common. Spiral galaxies, like our own, have curving arms and are still making new stars, while elliptical galaxies are smooth ovals made mostly of old red stars. Irregular galaxies have no clear shape at all, and some of them were torn out of shape by close encounters with their neighbours.

The Milky Way belongs to a small family of galaxies called the Local Group, which has at least 80 members, most of them tiny. Andromeda is the largest, the Milky Way is the second largest, and the third is a smaller spiral called Triangulum. Together they are held in one gravitational family, and they are slowly moving towards a common centre.

Collisions between galaxies are common, especially in the past, and the universe has seen countless of them. In the Antennae Galaxies, tens of millions of light-years away, two spirals are crashing together now, and their clouds of gas are being squeezed so hard that they have given birth to thousands of new star clusters. Noor said that, strangely, destruction and creation are often the same event in the universe.

Many galaxies gather in clusters of hundreds or thousands, such as the Virgo Cluster, which lies about 55 million light-years away. On the very largest scale, these clusters are joined by threads and sheets of galaxies in a cosmic web, with giant voids between them where there is almost nothing at all. Kit thought that the universe looked less like a collection of islands and more like a great sponge.

In December 1995 astronomers took a bold gamble: they pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a patch of sky that looked completely empty and kept it there for ten days. The patch was no bigger than a tennis ball seen from 100 metres away, yet the picture showed about 3,000 galaxies of every shape and colour. A later picture of a similar patch, taken with new cameras, revealed about 10,000 galaxies.

Noor asked Kit to multiply: if one tiny square holds thousands of galaxies, and the sky contains millions of such squares, how many galaxies must there be? The honest answer is that astronomers do not know exactly, but they estimate at least hundreds of billions in the part of the universe that we can see. Some studies suggest that there may be as many as a trillion or more.

Because light travels at a fixed speed, the farther away something is, the older its light is when it reaches us, and so a telescope is also a time machine. We see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago, Andromeda as it was two and a half million years ago, and the most distant galaxies as they were more than thirteen billion years ago. When Kit looked out of the Skylift window, he was reading the history of the universe.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021, carries a gold-coated mirror more than six metres wide, made of 18 hexagonal segments. It sees infrared light, which can pass through dust and which also carries the stretched light of the most distant galaxies. It has found galaxies that already existed only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, much earlier than most astronomers expected.

When astronomers split the light of a galaxy into a spectrum, they find that the colours of far galaxies are shifted towards the red end. This redshift is a sign that space is expanding, because the waves of light are stretched as they travel through it, much as the sound of a passing siren drops in pitch. The farther away a galaxy lies, the greater its redshift, and the faster it seems to be receding.

In 1929 Edwin Hubble published evidence that almost every galaxy is racing away from us, and that the more distant a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. Noor asked Kit to imagine dots drawn on a balloon: as the balloon is blown up, every dot moves away from every other, and none of them is at the centre. Space itself is stretching, and every galaxy sees the others moving away, which is why there is no centre to the expansion.

It is easy to wonder whether the expansion is stretching us too, but it is not. Atoms, people, planets and even whole galaxies are held together by forces that overpower the stretching, and the expansion matters only across the vast spaces between clusters of galaxies. Noor said that Kit could stop worrying that his trousers might be getting too short, and he laughed with relief.

There are two good ways of measuring the speed at which the universe is expanding: one uses stars and exploding stars in nearby galaxies, and the other uses the afterglow of the early universe. The two answers differ by several percent, which is more than the uncertainties in either measurement allow. This disagreement, known as the Hubble tension, may point to a mistake somewhere or to new physics that nobody has yet understood.

In 1927, two years before Hubble's famous paper, the Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre used Einstein's equations to show that the universe should be expanding, and he even estimated the rate. He went on to suggest that if the universe is growing now, it must once have been tiny, hot and dense, which was the first form of the Big Bang idea. Einstein was at first doubtful about the idea, but in time he came to admire the work.

Beyond a certain distance, about fourteen billion light-years, galaxies are carried away from us faster than light. This does not break Einstein's rule that nothing can travel through space faster than light, because it is space itself that is stretching, not the galaxies that are moving through it. Noor said that the lift, being imaginary, was now heading back towards the very beginning.

Noor said that they had reached the earliest moment that science can describe, the Big Bang, almost fourteen billion years ago. At that time, everything in the universe that we can see was packed into an unimaginably hot and dense state, and then it began to expand. It was not the birth of a new world in an old world, Noor said, but the beginning of space and time themselves.

It is tempting to picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off in the middle of empty space, but that picture is wrong. There was no outside for it to explode into, and no single place where it happened, because space itself was expanding everywhere at once. If Kit were to ask where the Big Bang took place, Noor said, the true answer would be: right here, and everywhere else too.

Kit could not help asking the obvious question: what happened before the Big Bang? Noor answered honestly that nobody knows, that our best theories stop working at that extreme moment, and that some scientists suspect the question may have no meaning if time itself began there. She added that a good scientist is not ashamed to say I do not know.

In the first second, the universe was a thick, glowing soup of tiny particles at a temperature far beyond anything that exists today. Many physicists believe that in the first fraction of a second, the universe went through a burst of incredibly fast growth called inflation, which stretched a region smaller than an atom to an enormous size. The evidence for this idea is good but not yet certain, and scientists are still testing it.

Within the first few minutes, the temperature fell enough for protons and neutrons to stick together and form the nuclei of the lightest elements. When this brief period of nuclear fusion ended, about three quarters of the ordinary matter was hydrogen and about one quarter was helium, with a trace of a few others. This is almost exactly the mixture that astronomers find in the oldest stars, which is strong support for the theory.

For hundreds of thousands of years after the Big Bang, space was filled with a hot, bright fog of electrons and nuclei, so thick that light could scarcely move through it. It was like being inside the glow of a sun, and no stars or planets existed yet. Noor said that the whole universe had been something like the inside of a star, only much calmer and more even.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled to about 3,000 degrees Celsius, cool enough for electrons to join with nuclei and form the first complete atoms. Suddenly the fog was gone, because light no longer bumped into free particles, and it was free to travel across the universe. Noor said that this was the moment when the universe first became transparent, and that the light has been travelling ever since.

That first light is still travelling, and it reaches us today from every direction in the sky. Over almost fourteen billion years, the stretching of space has turned it from bright glowing light into faint microwaves, which are known as the cosmic microwave background. A small share of the static on an old television set, tuned between channels, is this ancient light.

In 1965 two radio astronomers were testing a large horn antenna in New Jersey when they found a faint hiss that would not go away. They checked every wire and even cleaned out pigeon droppings, but the noise stayed, and it turned out to be the afterglow of the Big Bang. They received the Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery in 1978, and the antenna is now a historic landmark.

Space satellites such as COBE, WMAP and Planck have made detailed maps of the ancient light across the whole sky. The maps show tiny differences in temperature, only about one part in 100,000, which mark places where there was slightly more matter than average. Gravity pulled on those places for hundreds of millions of years, and they grew into the first stars and the galaxies that fill the sky today.

In 1933 the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky measured how fast the galaxies in a large cluster were moving, and he found that they moved far too quickly. The gravity of all the stars and gas that he could see was nowhere near enough to hold the cluster together, so he suggested that there must be a great deal of unseen matter. Most astronomers took little notice of this bold idea until the 1970s, when new evidence arrived.

In the 1970s the American astronomer Vera Rubin measured the speeds of stars as they circled in many different galaxies. In our own Solar System, the outer planets move more slowly than the inner ones, but in galaxies, the stars near the edge move just as fast as those near the centre. The simplest explanation is that each galaxy sits inside a huge halo of matter that gives off no light.

This unseen substance is called dark matter, because it neither gives out nor absorbs any light, and yet it exerts gravity like any other mass. There is about five times as much of it in the universe as there is ordinary matter, the kind from which stars, planets and people are made. Noor admitted that, for all that, scientists still do not know what it actually is.

The Bullet Cluster is the result of two groups of galaxies colliding at high speed. The hot gas was slowed down by the impact and stayed near the middle, but the way the clusters bend light showed that most of the mass carried straight on, as though nothing had happened. Many astronomers consider this one of the strongest pieces of evidence that dark matter really exists.

Physicists have built huge, sensitive detectors in mines deep underground, filled with liquid xenon, where cosmic rays cannot reach them, and they wait for a dark matter particle to bump into an atom. So far, none has been caught, and particle colliders have not made any either. Some scientists therefore wonder whether gravity itself needs to be changed, though most still think that dark matter is the better explanation.

Without dark matter, galaxies would probably not have had time to form, because ordinary matter alone clumped together too slowly. Dark matter began to gather into clumps earlier, and its gravity then pulled in clouds of ordinary gas, so that each galaxy grew inside a halo of dark matter like a pearl inside an oyster. The cosmic web of galaxies traces the pattern that the dark matter laid down long before the first star shone.

Noor explained that for the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang the universe was dark, with no stars at all. Then gravity gathered the first clouds of hydrogen and helium into the first stars, many of them probably far larger than the Sun and short-lived. They made the first heavy elements, and when they exploded, they began the long process of filling the universe with the ingredients for planets.

In 1998 two separate teams of astronomers measured the brightness of distant exploding stars, and both reached the same shocking conclusion. The expansion of the universe is not slowing down under the pull of gravity, as nearly everyone had assumed, but speeding up. The leaders of the two teams shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011, and the result is now widely accepted.

Scientists use the name dark energy for whatever is causing the expansion to speed up, and the name is really a way of admitting ignorance. One idea is that it is a built-in energy of empty space itself, which Einstein once added to his equations and later called a blunder. Observations in recent years hint that dark energy may change with time, but the evidence is not yet strong enough for anyone to be sure.

When astronomers add up everything, they find that ordinary matter, the stuff of every star, planet and person, makes up only about five percent of the universe. Dark matter accounts for about 27 percent and dark energy for about 68 percent, and neither is understood. New telescopes such as the European Euclid mission, launched in 2023, are now mapping billions of galaxies in the hope of finding out what these dark things really are.

Kit leaned against the glass and asked whether the universe came to an end somewhere, like the wall of a huge room. Noor shook her head and explained that what has an edge is our view, not necessarily the universe itself. The part we can see, she said, is called the observable universe, and it is only a small piece of everything.

Light from the most distant places has had only almost fourteen billion years to reach us, because the universe is that young. During all that time, however, space has kept stretching, so the matter that sent the oldest light is now about 46 billion light-years from us. These numbers sound impossible at first, but they follow naturally from the idea of an expanding universe.

Beyond the limit of our view, light from other regions has not had time to arrive, and some of it may never reach us at all. There is no evidence that the universe stops at that invisible line, so most astronomers expect it to continue. We are in the position of a sailor who can see only as far as the horizon, although the sea goes on.

Measurements of the ancient microwave glow show that space is flat, as far as anyone can tell, with only a tiny margin of error. A flat universe could be infinite, but it could also be enormous and finite, so this fact alone cannot settle the question. For now, Noor admitted, the honest answer to whether the universe goes on forever is that nobody knows.

Noor told Kit that astronomers estimate there are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on all the beaches of Earth. Nobody has counted them one by one, naturally, so the figure is an estimate built from careful samples of the sky. Even so, she added, it gives a feeling for how much there is to explore.

Kit held out his hand and found nothing there, which Noor said was exactly the point. Spread across the whole universe, ordinary matter amounts to less than one atom in every cubic metre, and the stars and planets are rare islands in an enormous emptiness. It is a humbling thought that we live on one of those islands, and a wonderful one too.

If dark energy stays as it is today, the distant galaxies will be carried away until their light can never reach us again. Our own neighbourhood will hold together, though, and the merged Milky Way and Andromeda, which some people nickname Milkomeda, will become a lonely island of stars. Future astronomers there might not even know that other galaxies ever existed, and they would see only darkness around them.

New stars will go on forming for trillions of years, and the faint red dwarfs will glow for even longer than that. Eventually, however, the gas will be spent and the last embers will cool, and the universe will become cold and dark. Noor said that this is only one possibility, since nobody knows for certain how the story ends.

So far nobody has found life anywhere except on Earth, and Noor was careful to say that no one knows whether it exists elsewhere. The ingredients are common, though, and there are billions of planets, so rovers search Mars for traces of ancient microbes and radio telescopes listen for signals from space. Nothing has been confirmed, but the search has only just begun, and the answer would change everything.

Kit wrote in his notebook that the edge of what we know has never stayed still. Even now astronomers are building the Extremely Large Telescope on a mountain in Chile, with a mirror about 39 metres across, and they hope it will show more of the early universe and of the planets around other stars. Every generation, Noor said, has pushed that edge a little further out, and the next one will do the same.
